text: The most famous of the new buildings sits right in the middle of 55th Street.
The University Apartments, two ten-story slabs designed by I.M.
Pei, finished in 1961, standing on a wide median between 1401 and 1451 East 55th Street.
Construction started in August of 1958, before the City Council had even approved the larger plan.
Pei put the towers on a long landscaped island in the road, with a parking garage underneath and a garden between them.
It's a serious piece of modern architecture, and it sits exactly where a dense, messy, mixed-race commercial strip used to be.
Nearby, in the Hyde Park A project, Pei's firm also put up rows of low row houses that people nicknamed the toasters, clean modern homes priced for buyers, not for the renters who'd been cleared.
The towers and the toasters are the plan in physical form.
Open, expensive, deliberate, and built on top of what was cleared.
The Hyde Park A and B projects alone displaced more than fifteen thousand residents.
Across the entire renewal area, the numbers tell the same story the towers do.
The neighborhood's Black population fell by about forty percent.
The median income climbed sharply, by something close to seventy percent.
Hyde Park became wealthier, whiter than it was heading toward being, and stable.
It also became more controlled.
Julian Levi and the South East Chicago Commission didn't go away after the bulldozers left.
They kept watch over property, over who bought what, over the conditions of buildings, for decades.
Hyde Park is one of the few genuinely integrated neighborhoods on the South Side.
It's also a neighborhood whose integration was engineered, and paid for, by removing the people who couldn't afford the result.
The families who left didn't vanish.
Many landed in already crowded Black neighborhoods to the south and west, where the same forces that had pushed them once would push them again.
Renewal in one place was pressure somewhere else, and the somewhere else rarely had a university to write its laws.
